item.title: Victoria’s Secret Brings Back the Fantasy Bra — and an Old Stereotype of Sexy
item.description:
The big reveal of the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show came about three-quarters of the way through the extravaganza.

It came after Bella Hadid had strutted out in stilettos, a bejeweled bra with matching panties and wings made to resemble a pointillist garden, like some sort of Seurat-inspired boudoir mirage. After Megan Moroney, in baby pink marabou wings, had serenaded a section featuring supermodels as sexy flower fairies and Tate McRae had writhed around in a crimson corset and matching stockings amid a sea of similarly writhing women in crimson lingerie.

It came after the “Pink” section, with Katseye as naughty schoolgirls and Trinity Rodman in sequined hot pants and a push-up bra. (Also, oddly, a lot of puppy dog handbags and puppy dog charms, because, apparently, we are no longer stereotyping young women as sex kittens and are now stereotyping them as … sex puppies? Progress!)

And the unveiling came with a lot of dramatic backlighting to build anticipation. Then, finally: ta-da!

The Fantasy Bra: a $50 million creation by Jacob Arabo of Jacob & Co. featuring a 75.54-carat vivid yellow diamond amid 4,410 white diamonds, modeled by Kylie Jenner, with her own set of unicorn-like wings and a wisp of a sheer miniskirt, for modesty. Or at least the suggestion of it.

It was the first time a fantasy bra, once the centerpiece of the show, had been seen on a Victoria’s Secret runway since 2018.

As such, it was the final variable in a return to form for Victoria’s Secret that has been taking shape over the past two years. First, the brand brought back the runway, which was canceled in 2019 as ties between Les Wexner, then the company’s owner, and Jeffrey Epstein, were exposed, and then revived in 2024). Then it brought back the Angels, who were retired in 2021 in favor of a woman-focused collective, then unretired two years ago. It even brought back Gisele Bündchen, the most famous Angel of all, who made a cameo video languorously reclining on her sofa in little lacy nothings before this year’s show. (There were rumors that she was going to walk the runway, but a broken foot just beforehand seemed to put an end to that.) And it brought the show back to Los Angeles for the first time in nearly 20 years.

But in bringing back the Fantasy Bra, the brand’s leaders weren’t just revealing an extravagant new piece of intimate couture. They were revealing just how much we have reverted to pre-#MeToo definitions of sexy and how little change has actually occurred, despite all of the soul-searching and existential crises of the early 2020s about how a brand that put women on display like dream dolls of the bedroom may have contributed to a culture of sexual harassment and abuse. Amid all of the hooting and catcalling for Jenner, including by her boyfriend, Timothée Chalamet, and her mother, Kris Jenner, both sitting in the front row, that disappearing idea may have been the most transparent look of all.

It’s almost as if the past seven years didn’t happen.

After all, VS may position the show as an expression of self-confidence and joy. The chief executive, Hillary Super, and Adam Selman, the creative director, may talk about giving women ownership of their own bodies, and there may be a variety of those bodies on display, with Nicole Kidman cheering on from the front row. But there’s no getting away from the reality that the VS show is perpetrating a very specific Vargas girl-Playboy tradition of sexy.

One that is all about the legs! And the boobs! And the bottom! It’s cloaking the promise of transgression in the trappings of the cherub, then putting it on display for everyone to see.

According to Selman, this is all in the service of what the VS customer wants. VS decided to bring back the Fantasy Bra because fans were asking for it, he said. He christened this year’s show, which also included a performance by Megan Thee Stallion, “Fandemonium.” And it’s clearly working: The company’s share price has surged this year.

So maybe the whole bustier-’n-knickers babe look is most women’s dream, as it clearly was most men’s. By reverting to these old gender stereotypes, VS is reverting to a time when “sexy” was defined by the male gaze and catering to it. The company may have changed its stock market ticker listing to VSXY from VSCO in June to reflect its new mission, but there is nothing particularly new about this idea.

Or maybe what this is about is a nostalgia for a time when we could pretend that this way of presenting women was just lighthearted fun and didn’t contribute directly to a culture that enabled their objectification and depersonalization — even though we know that such a time is as much a fantasy as the fantasy bra. Watching the VS show after the national conversation prompted by the crisis at Cornell is a bit like entering the twilight zone. Though it does go with another national conversation, one in which men are men and women are women and you can tell by how they dress.

But here’s the thing: Victoria’s Secret may make undergarments, but they are still garments. It is still a fashion brand. And fashion is at its best when it gives people the thing they didn’t know they wanted: the thing that offers them a new, powerful way to be themselves in the world.

Wouldn’t it be incredible if, rather than simply reviving the past and resorting to sexy clichés, Selman and co. managed to think of a new way to communicate physical agency and unfetter the body? If what everyone saw on the VS runway wasn’t what they were expecting but a whole new idea about lingerie entirely?

Maybe that’s the real fantasy. If they could pull it off, this particular fashion form might actually take wing.

item.title: Trump Announces $8 Billion Plan to Cover Farm Losses
item.description:
President Trump said at a rally in Kansas Monday night that the Agriculture Department would provide $8 billion in economic aid to farmers hurt by high diesel prices.

It was the second time in two years that the president authorized billions of dollars in bailout money for farmers harmed by his administration’s policies, and came 15 days before a midterm election in which unhappy farmers and ranchers could be the deciding votes in close races across the country.

Under the plan, known as the Harvest Fuel Relief Program, the Agriculture Department will use a formula based on how many acres and which crops farmers planted to reimburse them for a “portion” of their losses. The money will come from the Commodity Credit Corporation, a financing institution that the Agriculture Department uses to fund crop insurance and natural disaster payment programs.

Payment rates will be announced next month, and farmers will receive money at a later date.

Farmers use diesel in their machinery and irrigation systems, especially in the fall when they run combine harvesters. The price of a gallon of diesel has averaged $6 or more in most of the country in recent weeks, compared with about $3.50 last fall, saddling many farmers with thousands of dollars in additional costs.

Higher diesel prices have hit farmers unevenly. According to the Farm Bureau, a lobby group, the production cost to grow an acre of wheat rose by $6 because of higher fuel costs, while the cost to grow an acre of rice rose by $52. Fertilizer costs, which are closely tied to fuel costs, also went up this spring and summer.

Farmers are traditionally a solid Republican voting bloc. But high fuel and fertilizer costs, along with tariffs and trade disruptions, are dragging down the electoral prospects of a number of Republican candidates in what were thought to be solidly Republican areas.

Mr. Trump was rallying for Senator Roger Marshall, a Kansas Republican, outside of Wichita on Monday night. Mr. Marshall comfortably won election in 2020 by 11 points, but most polls show the he is tied or running slightly behind his Democratic challenger, Adam Hamilton. National Republican groups have been diverting money to Kansas to shore up Mr. Marshall’s chances.

In announcing the aid for farmers, Mr. Trump sought to credit it to Mr. Marshall. “Roger Marshall is the leader who fought for that to happen,” he said.

Neither the president nor the Agriculture Department explained the causes of higher diesel prices:

During the early months of the war in Iran, oil exports through the Persian Gulf nearly ground to a halt, driving up prices. The flow of oil and refined fuel has resumed — with the help of the U.S. military — but volumes are still below prewar levels.

The rescue package came two weeks after the president announced a more modest executive order to help farmers with high diesel prices at a rally in a different Midwest farm state, Nebraska.

That order allowed the use so-called dyed diesel — which typically can only be used in off-road machinery like tractors — in on-road vehicles, and defers and possibly eliminates some taxes on it. The amount of money that farmers were estimated to save from the dyed diesel order was far less than the $8 billion they were set to receive through the Harvest Fuel Relief Program.

The latest rescue package mirrored the $12 billion Farmer Bridge Assistance Program the Agriculture Department rolled out in December. That was called an “economic loss program” and came after months of lower-than-usual exports of American crops because of the Trump administration’s tariff and trade policies.

item.title: Boeing’s Large 737 Max Jet Secures U.S. Approval
item.description:
Boeing won regulatory approval for the largest version of the 737 Max on Tuesday after a six-year delay. The certification of the plane, the Boeing 737 Max 10, clears the way for Boeing to try to catch up with Airbus, its European rival, which became the world’s top airplane manufacturer in recent years.

“After extensive safety reviews — including thousands of hours of test flights — the team at the F.A.A. is ready to approve this critical aircraft for sale,” the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, said in a statement. “This is a major win for American manufacturing and our nation’s status as a global aviation powerhouse.”

Planes are certified in the United States by the Federal Aviation Administration, which is part of Mr. Duffy’s department.

The Max 10 is already an important part of Boeing’s portfolio of commercial planes, with more than 1,550 orders for the plane, accounting for more than 30 percent of the company’s outstanding Max orders.

Airlines have increasingly favored larger planes like the Max 10 to cater to rising global travel demand and manage congestion at airports. The Max 7, the smallest in the plane family, was approved in early August. The Max 7 can carry up to 172 passengers compared with 230 for the Max 10.

The Max 10 was originally expected to be certified in 2020, but approval was delayed for several reasons, including two fatal crashes of the 737 Max 8 in 2018 and 2019 in which 346 people died. Those crashes led to a nearly two-year global ban on Max flights.

Boeing suffered another setback in 2024 when a panel blew off a Max 9 plane during a flight. To win approval for the Max 10, Boeing also had to make some safety retrofits and redesign the jet’s engine anti-icing system.

The announcement on Tuesday clears the way for Boeing to begin delivering the Max 10, which Boeing has started producing. The first deliveries are expected in the coming months.

“Completing the certification program clears the path for us to deliver a Boeing airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation,” said Stephanie Pope, the chief executive of Boeing’s commercial airplanes unit.

The company completed the final Max 10 certification flight this summer, ending a testing campaign that included 976 flights in all. United Airlines, Alaska Airlines and Ryanair, the European carrier, are among the biggest buyers of the Max 10.

Boeing has fallen well behind Airbus in recent years in selling narrow-body planes like the 737 and the Airbus A320. More than 10,200 Airbus narrow-body planes are in active use worldwide, compared with 8,200 Boeings, according to Cirium. Airbus has amassed orders for more than 8,200 narrow-body planes, and Boeing has about 5,000. The last time there were more narrow-body Boeing jets in use than Airbus planes was in 2017.

item.title: Netflix Is Great at Making Money. Its Problem Is Keeping Viewers Hooked.
item.description:
After a tumultuous week, when Netflix laid off 1,000 employees and fired its chief content officer and top two film executives, the world’s largest streaming service showed that one thing isn’t in flux: its ability to make boatloads of money.

The company said on Tuesday that its revenues in the third quarter grew 12 percent from a year earlier, to nearly $12.9 billion, while net income rose 48 percent, to nearly $3.7 billion. For the year, Netflix said, it expects revenue growth to be 13 percent, roughly in line with its previous estimates.

But the company also acknowledged the undercurrent that led to the recent tumult: concern about stagnating attention time on its service.

“We know there’s some investor concern about our view-hours growth,” particularly in the United States and Canada, Netflix told investors in a letter. Revenue in those countries grew 11 percent in the most recent quarter, down from 17 percent a year earlier.

Still, the company reiterated that by executing on its strategy for growth — delivering “differentiated, exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events” while trying to bring “more third-party content to its service” — it will boost engagement time.

Netflix delivered its quarterly results while at a crossroads. Despite being the most-watched paid streaming service in the world, with 325 million subscribers, the company is not growing fast enough for either its top executives or its shareholders.

The time that viewers spend on the service has stagnated, as YouTube increasingly becomes a competitor. Netflix has struggled to create a pipeline of new hits to replace shows like “Stranger Things” and “Squid Game.” Returning shows like “Beef,” “The Night Agent” and “Avatar: The Last Airbender” lost significant viewership for their most recent seasons, according to Netflix’s metrics.

And no film released this summer became a breakout hit, a contrast with last summer, when “KPop Demon Hunters” and “Happy Gilmore 2” captivated viewers. Indeed, the company’s biggest film hit for the quarter was “The Last House,” which generated 91 million views but scored dismally with both critics and audiences.

Netflix’s stock has been on a slide since September last year, when it announced its intention to purchase Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming business in a nearly $83 billion deal. Even after the company bowed out of the pursuit, not willing to get in a bidding war with the eventual victor, Paramount Skydance, the stock continued to languish. Its price is down nearly 45 percent from a year ago.

Still, last week’s shake-up jolted Hollywood. A day after Netflix announced it was cutting 6 percent of its work force, it fired Bela Bajaria, a well-respected company veteran who, as chief content officer the past three years, expanded Netflix beyond scripted TV shows and movies into reality shows, live events, sports and video podcasts.

Peter Rice, a film and television executive who spent 30 years at Fox before becoming a top executive at Disney, has taken her place.

One of his first decisions will be choosing a top film executive to replace Dan Lin, who was fired late Friday after two and a half years at the company. Mr. Lin’s mandate to lower production costs and be more selective about what the streaming service makes faced great resistance by the talent. The directors Noah Baumbach and David Fincher ended their relationships with the company.

According to a letter that Mr. Lin sent to his team on his departure, which was obtained by The New York Times, the 53-year-old executive accomplished many of his goals. “For our film slate the past two years, per-title views are up 12 percent and view hours are up 11 percent,” he wrote, adding that in the first half of 2026, 10 of Netflix’s 13 films were rated “loved” by subscribers.

He leaves behind a robust slate of movies, including “The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” — a sequel of sorts to “Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood,” with a script from Quentin Tarantino and directed by Mr. Fincher. It will receive a two-week exclusive IMAX run this year, as will Pete Berg’s war drama, “The Mosquito Bowl.” Next year will bring “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew,” directed by Greta Gerwig (“Barbie”), and an animated “Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory”

Many in Hollywood are curious whether Mr. Rice will expand Netflix’s tentative foray into releasing films in theaters before they appear on the service. Ted Sarandos, the company’s co-chief executive, has for years insisted that theatrical distribution is “an outmoded idea,” and that Netflix movies are made for its subscribers.

This past weekend, in a first, the company reported box office grosses for “La Bola Negra,” a Spanish-language multigenerational epic that it acquired at the Cannes Film Festival. The film will remain in theaters for 45 days before it debuts on the service.

Netflix’s television team has also been busy buying up projects over the last year. The streamer gave a straight-to-series order to “The Corrections,” an adaptation of Jonathan Franzen’s 2001 novel, with Meryl Streep expected to star and Cord Jefferson (the writer and director of “American Fiction”) expected to direct the limited series. Netflix also ordered “Rabbit, Rabbit,” a thriller starring Adam Driver and Regina Hall that is expected to premiere next year.

Production also began recently on an adaptation of the Dan Brown novel “The Secret of Secrets.” Carlton Cuse (“Lost,” “Jack Ryan”) is the showrunner, and it stars Morgan Spector (“The Gilded Age”).

The company is banking on these movies and shows, and Mr. Rice’s changes, to reverse the trend of subscribers’ engagement with its offerings. Netflix accounted for 7.8 percent of all television viewing time in the United States in July, according to Nielsen, a full percentage point drop from a year earlier. YouTube’s share was more than 14 percent.

Despite all the turmoil, Netflix maintains a loyal following. According to a report released on Tuesday by Antenna, Netflix has the lowest churn numbers, or cancellation rate, of any streamer.

John Koblin contributed reporting from New York

item.title: SpaceX Swings to a Profit, as A.I. Business Grows
item.description:
Since Elon Musk took SpaceX public in June, he has increasingly made the rocket company the center of his business empire.

Mr. Musk recently weighed in on the war in Ukraine when SpaceX limited its satellite internet service in the country. He has used hundreds of millions of dollars, fueled partly by his fortune from SpaceX, to fund Republican groups ahead of the midterm elections. And on Monday, he pledged one share of SpaceX to “every kid in America” next year through a government-operated savings account program championed by President Trump.

On Tuesday, SpaceX showed why it continues to be a source of Mr. Musk’s influence: The company’s quarterly sales soared, driven by a fast-growing artificial intelligence business. The tech billionaire also said SpaceX and Tesla, his electric car company, were exploring a merger, which would consolidate his empire.

In its second earnings report as a public company, SpaceX said revenue for the three months that ended Sept. 30 was $14.5 billion, more than 2.5 times as much as the $5.6 billion from a year earlier. Profit totaled $4.4 billion, or 37 cents per share, compared with a net loss of $1.05 billion last year. The numbers surpassed Wall Street projections of $13 billion in revenue and profit of 16 cents a share.

How much SpaceX is spending on A.I. — which includes its Grok chatbot and data centers — was particularly scrutinized. The company said its capital expenditures had risen to $19.6 billion, nearly three times the $6.9 billion from a year earlier. And SpaceX is likely to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the current quarter, Bret Johnsen, the company’s chief financial officer, told investors on Tuesday.

Still, A.I. has become the largest part of SpaceX’s business, with the technology’s revenue — $7.6 billion — exceeding what the company is generating from space launches and its Starlink satellite internet service.

“I’ve never seen anything grow this fast,” Mr. Musk said during a call with investors, referring to Grok Bot, an A.I. agent created by the company that can autonomously complete tasks that users assign to it. Mr. Musk, who has often been overambitious in his business goals, said he envisioned that SpaceX’s revenue would continue to accelerate, reaching “between $500 billion and $1 trillion” by the end of 2027.

Mr. Musk also addressed speculation that he would merge SpaceX with Tesla, which is reporting earnings on Wednesday. He said that the two companies had formed committees to discuss the idea and that he had not participated because of the conflict of interest.

“At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” Mr. Musk said, adding that he thought the idea had “a lot of merit.”

SpaceX’s stock rose more than 5 percent in after-hours trading. Its shares are trading above their $135 initial public offering price, but have swung up and down.

SpaceX’s performance on the stock market is a barometer for Anthropic, the A.I. company that may go public as early as next month. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, is also preparing for an initial public offering, which could come next year. SpaceX’s results are viewed as offering clues to the direction of the A.I. industry, which has faced questions over whether the spending and borrowing by data center companies such as CoreWeave and Oracle can be sustained.

Melissa Otto, who leads a research group at S&P Global, said she expected SpaceX’s capital expenditures to increase to nearly $195 billion by 2028 from about $70 billion this year. Spending “is what the market is very focused on right now,” she said.

Jacob Bourne, an analyst with eMarketer, said SpaceX could further differentiate itself in A.I. with “its longer-term ambitions to build data centers in space,” but these efforts require large sums and face “enormous technical and practical challenges.”

SpaceX said revenue from its A.I. business had grown to $7.6 billion in the quarter from $813 million a year earlier. The company attributed the growth to deals it struck to lease its computing power to others, as well as the August acquisition of Cursor, an A.I.-powered coding service. Mr. Musk said he was being “hounded relentlessly” by other A.I. companies that want to rent computing power.

SpaceX added that Starlink had 13.6 million consumer subscribers, along with hundreds of thousands of enterprise customers. The satellite internet service generated $5.2 billion in revenue, up 69 percent from $3.1 billion a year earlier.

Revenue in the space business grew more modestly, rising 6 percent to $1.8 billion. The company said it was continuing to book launches and was developing a new Starbase spaceport in Louisiana, which is set to begin operating in 2029.

Jack Ewing contributed reporting.

item.title: Britain Is Said to Approve New Gas Drilling in the North Sea
item.description:
The British government is set announce on Wednesday the approval of a major new natural gas drilling project in the North Sea, according to two people briefed on the announcement.

The gas field, known as Jackdaw and located off the coast of Scotland, would be the site of the first gas extraction in the North Sea since a government moratorium on new drilling was imposed in 2024. The approval is expected to face criticism from environmental groups, which have said any new fossil fuel production would undermine Britain’s climate change pledges.

An application to drill for oil at a separate field known as Rosebank, off the Shetland coast of Scotland, was still under consideration, according to the two people, who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the announcement.

A spokesman for Andy Burnham, the prime minister, declined to comment. A spokeswoman for Britain’s Department of Energy Security and Net Zero said the agency intended to make an announcement on Wednesday but declined to provide details.

A spokesman for Adura, a joint venture between Shell, the British oil giant, and the Norwegian energy company Equinor, declined to comment on Tuesday. Equinor wants to develop both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

The Jackdaw gas field holds an estimated 200 million barrels of oil equivalent, which would be used in Britain and fed into the gas network. The approval of the project would represent a recognition of Britain’s continued reliance on natural gas even as it moves toward greater use of renewable energy.

Mr. Burnham, who took office in July, built his reputation as a populist champion for a green industrial transition, and approving major new oil and gas fields is expected to create significant friction with his supporters. He has faced pressure from the oil and gas industry and from President Trump to approve drilling at both Jackdaw and Rosebank.

The war in Iran has disrupted global energy markets, pushing up the cost of imported oil and gas. Britain imports most of its oil and gas. Supporters of new drilling in the North Sea argue that expanding domestic production is essential to safeguarding Britain’s energy security and shielding households from price volatility.

Adura estimated that Jackdaw’s gas could meet roughly 6 percent of Britain’s total gas needs and heat 1.4 million homes.

Supporters of new drilling argue that even as Britain transitions to clean energy, the nation will remain dependent on natural gas for decades. After all, 85 percent of Britain’s homes and businesses still use boilers for hot water and central heating, and 30 million vehicles still run on petroleum. New domestic sources will help ease Britain’s reliance on imports.

John Underhill, director for energy transition at Aberdeen University in Scotland, said approval of drilling at Jackdaw would be “a timely and welcome boost for the oil and gas sector and the U.K. as the country faces a challenging winter.”

Environmental groups have estimated Jackdaw’s gas will serve closer to 2 percent of the country’s needs and noted that Britain would still require imports. They also maintained that new oil and gas extraction takes money and momentum away from renewable power.

Michael D. Shear contributed reporting.

item.title: Britain Approves New Gas Drilling in the North Sea
item.description:
The British government greenlit a major offshore natural gas project in the North Sea on Wednesday, defying its own climate change pledge to halt new fossil fuel extraction.

The approval for the Jackdaw field, off the coast of Scotland, is a major victory for Britain’s oil and gas industry, unions and cities in Britain’s energy heartland, which consider the project an economic lifeline. It is also a win for President Trump, who has pressured a succession of British leaders to “open up” the North Sea to new oil and gas drilling.

Amid a sharp rise in energy prices caused by the war in Iran, British leaders cast the decision as a crucial step toward reducing the country’s reliance on imported fuels. Jackdaw’s gas would be used in Britain and fed into the gas network.

“We’re committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050,” Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said in a statement. But, he added, “Even on our ambitious climate path, we’ll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That’s why we’re taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea.”

Mr. Burnham also on Wednesday announced the creation of a government fund to support renewable energy. According to the energy ministry, the fund will begin with 2 billion pounds (about $2.6 billion) in funds with future revenue from offshore drilling feeding into it over time.

Environmental activists called the approval of Jackdaw a betrayal of the country’s efforts to transition to renewable energy. They noted that the decision comes weeks ahead of a United Nations climate summit in Turkey, where Mr. Burnham has said he will lead the British delegation and “meet the climate challenge.”

This week the United Nations reported that the world needs to cut greenhouse gas emissions — created mostly by the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas — by nearly a fifth in the next four years to avoid the most dangerous consequences of climate change.

“Jackdaw won’t make a lot of difference to our energy bills, but it will fuel the climate chaos already unfurling in front of us,” said Danny Gross, a campaigner for Friends of the Earth, an environmental group.

Mr. Burnham’s government has left an even more contentious decision — whether to allow a separate offshore oil development in the North Sea known as Rosebank — for a later date.

Jackdaw will be the first new oil and gas extraction in Britain’s North Sea since the Labour government imposed a moratorium on new drilling in 2024.

Adura, a joint venture between Shell, the British oil giant, and the Norwegian energy company Equinor, intends to develop the project. It has said work on the field could begin immediately after approval

Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura, urged Mr. Burnham to also approve the Rosebank project.

“Taken together, Jackdaw and Rosebank offer significant benefits for the U.K.,” Mr. McCulloch said in a statement. At their peaks, he said, the projects could provide around 10 percent of the country’s domestic gas and oil production.

Britain imports most of its oil and gas, and the war in Iran has pushed up the costs by disrupting global energy markets. Supporters of new North Sea drilling argue that expanding domestic extraction is essential to safeguarding Britain’s energy security and shielding households from price volatility.

Adura estimated that Jackdaw’s gas could meet 6 percent of Britain’s gas needs and heat 1.4 million homes, reducing the country’s reliance on imported liquefied natural gas. The field is believed to hold gas equivalent to about 200 million barrels of oil.

Supporters of new drilling argue that even as Britain transitions to clean energy, the nation will remain dependent on natural gas for decades. After all, 85 percent of Britain’s homes and businesses still use boilers for hot water and central heating, and 30 million vehicles still run on petroleum. New domestic sources will help ease Britain’s reliance on imports.

While a portion of those imports comes via pipeline from Norway — a neighbor with strict environmental regulations — the rest must be shipped across oceans as liquefied natural gas, or L.N.G. Supplying Britain from far-flung producers like Qatar, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago carries a significantly higher carbon footprint because of the energy required to cool and transport the gas.

“Jackdaw is 99.9 percent complete and with approval now secured, gas from this field will be flowing into homes up and down the country within weeks,” Russell Borthwick, chief executive of the Aberdeen & Grampian Chamber of Commerce said in a statement.

He called the approval “a direct, tangible boost to the U.K.’s energy security at a time when it matters most.”

Environmental groups have estimated Jackdaw’s gas will serve closer to 2 percent of the country’s needs and noted that Britain would still require imports. They also maintained that new oil and gas extraction diverts money and momentum from renewable power.

“Jackdaw has been oversold,” said Tessa Khan, the executive director of Uplift, a British environmental group.

“Clean energy is how we lower bills and reindustrialize regions, not by caving to an oil industry making obscene profits while pushing up bills, laying off workers and driving the heat waves we saw this summer,” Ms. Khan said.

There is also the question of whether the approval of Jackdaw violates domestic and international commitments.

Rosebank was first approved in 2022 and Jackdaw a year later, when the Conservative Party was in power. But environmental groups sued, and those approvals were later overturned.

In 2024, nearly 200 nations agreed at a United Nations climate summit to transition away from fossil fuels. A few months later, the Labour government under Keir Starmer, who preceded Mr. Burnham, pledged a moratorium on new drilling licenses.

Mr. Burnham inherited that pledge when he became prime minister in July. But since both fields were licensed under a previous government, supporters argued, allowing exploration to move forward again does not violate the moratorium.

For the fog-shrouded stretch of the Scottish coastline around Aberdeen, the epicenter of Britain’s oil industry, the approval offers a new economic opportunity. The region has endured a quarter-century of declining North Sea production, with the local business chamber reporting losses of more than 1,000 oil and gas jobs each month.

The anxiety over the basin’s decline was underscored in August when BP announced plans to sell its North Sea business after six decades of operations there.

Oil and gas industry officials said the approval of Jackdaw was unlikely to change BP’s decision. It also won’t change the fundamental geology of the North Sea basin, where about 93 percent of oil and gas has already been extracted.

But, they argued, the project would provide enough investment to keep jobs steady as Britain sought to bolster renewable energy industries like offshore wind.

For Mr. Burnham, the decision is one of the first tests of how he will balance demands from progressive lawmakers in his party with the economic realities that face his government.

Many Labour members of Parliament are counting on Mr. Burnham to be a more robust supporter of their pro-environment agenda than Mr. Starmer was. During two decades in public life, Mr. Burnham has frequently endorsed net-zero policies and vowed to be part of the fight against climate change.

But the wars in Ukraine and Iran have driven up the price of energy and left many in the country angry about the rising cost of living.

Those goals — maintaining his party’s commitment to the environment and promising to lower energy costs — could prove difficult to achieve at the same time. Since Mr. Burnham took office, his aides have suggested he will take a “pragmatic” approach to energy, by accepting the need for dependence on fossil fuels in the short run but pushing the country toward a sustainable transition over time.

In his first call as prime minister with President Trump, Mr. Burnham also promised that he would be pragmatic about the North Sea energy fields. “There is a resource there,” the prime minister told reporters. “When people are struggling, we can’t ignore that.”

In some ways, Mr. Burnham’s decision to approve new drilling is a strange alignment with Mr. Trump, who has berated British prime ministers for embracing net-zero policies and failing to drill more in the North Sea.

Despite Mr. Trump’s vocal support for British offshore extraction, American oil giants have almost entirely abandoned the North Sea, driven out by declining yields in mature fields and higher operating costs.

ConocoPhillips sold off its British fields in 2019, followed by Exxon Mobil, which parted with decades of North Sea holdings to refocus capital on U.S. shale and South American deepwater projects. Chevron, the last major American holdout, also sold its remaining British North Sea assets.

Michael D. Shear contributed reporting from London.
